extracted.intended_audience: Federal agencies, regulated parties, stakeholders, and members of the public interested in U.S. federal rulemaking and information-collection review
extracted.subtask_description: FAQ-style guidance on OIRA's role in federal rulemaking and Paperwork Reduction Act information-collection review, including definitions, procedural steps, evaluation criteria, transparency policies, and how the public participates. Useful for agencies preparing rules/ICRs and for stakeholders wishing to comment or meet with OIRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation is a general statement issued by an agency, board, or commission that has the force and effect of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains that Congress often grants agencies authority to issue regulations; regulations specify details and requirements necessary to implement and enforce legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rulemaking process under the APA
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal regulations are created through 'rulemaking' governed by the Administrative Procedure Act (5 U.S.C. Chapter 5).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process: agency develops and typically publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register soliciting public comments; after considering comments and making changes, it publishes a final rule and must describe and respond to public comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA generally requires agencies to provide public notice and seek comment prior to enacting new regulations and sets out procedures for judicial review of rules in federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frames the legal baseline for public notice/comment and judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional role and Congressional Review Act (CRA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress enacts laws that mandate or authorize agencies to issue regulations and uses oversight (hearings, reports, legislation) including the CRA to review and possibly reject new regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CRA requires agencies to submit all new final rules to both House and Senate; Congress may reconsider and vote to overturn a rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Register role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Register is the official daily publication for agency rules, proposed rules, and notices, published by the Office of the Federal Register (NARA).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies publish proposed and final rules there; the Federal Register is the place to find notices seeking public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA's role in rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA (Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs) reviews draft proposed and final regulations under Executive Order 12866 and develops/oversees government-wide policies on information, privacy, and statistical policy; reviews information collections under the PRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA coordinates interagency Executive Branch review of significant regulations to ensure compliance with EO 12866 principles, incorporation of public comment, consideration of alternatives, and cost-benefit analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866 principles
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 12866 establishes objectives and principles (enhance planning and coordination, reaffirm agency primacy, restore integrity of regulatory review, make process accessible/open) and requires analysis of costs and benefits and reasoned determinations that benefits justify costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For significant regulatory actions OIRA review is required; agencies must analyze costs and benefits and act on the basis of a reasoned determination. EO 12866 also requires agencies to consider public comment and alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a 'significant' regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EO 12866, 'significant' actions are those that: (1) have an annual effect on the economy of $100M+ or materially affect economy/public sectors; (2) create serious inconsistency with other agencies; (3) materially alter budgetary impact of programs or rights/obligations of recipients; or (4) raise novel legal or policy issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant regulatory actions must be reviewed by OIRA and agencies must provide an explanation of need and an assessment of costs and benefits. OIRA designates ~500–700 regulatory actions as significant each year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'economically significant' regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Economically significant' actions are a subset of significant actions likely to have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or materially affect the economy/public health/environment/etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For economically significant rules, EO 12866 directs agencies to provide more detailed, quantified assessments of likely benefits and costs and analyses of effective and reasonably feasible alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review timeframe limits
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA review period is limited by EO 12866 to 90 days; there is no minimum period. The head of the rulemaking agency may extend review indefinitely; the OMB Director may extend on a one-time basis for up to 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sets procedural timing expectations for agency drafts under OIRA review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning and grounds for OIRA 'returns' of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA may 'return' a rule to the agency for reconsideration if the rule is not compatible with the law, the quality of the agency's analysis is inadequate, the regulation is not justified by the analysis, it is inconsistent with EO 12866 principles or Presidential priorities, or it conflicts with other Executive Branch efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Return letters explain why further consideration is recommended; a return does not necessarily imply OIRA/OMB opposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency withdrawal of rules during OIRA review
rubrics_metrics.description: At any time during OIRA review an agency may withdraw its rule from review and choose not to move forward or to resubmit after further consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interested parties may contact the agency regarding specific withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purposes of regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis helps anticipate and evaluate the likely consequences of rules (costs and benefits), to determine if benefits justify costs, to promote public accountability, and to identify alternatives that maximize net benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful analysis can demonstrate when less stringent alternatives are preferable, or when greater stringency is justified; other laws (Regulatory Flexibility Act, Unfunded Mandates Reform Act) also require such evaluations for certain rulemakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB Circular A-4 guidance on regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB's Circular A-4 ('Regulatory Analysis') defines good regulatory analysis and standardizes measurement and reporting of benefits and costs; it provides technical guidance and best practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 was peer-reviewed and solicited public comments before finalization; agencies should follow its practices for strong analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA disclosure and transparency policies
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA makes public substantive communications with any party outside the Executive Branch concerning regulatory actions under review; meeting subject, date, participants, and written material received are disclosed and a meeting log is kept on Reginfo.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft documents under review are deliberative and not available for public release during review; after publication in the Federal Register, certain documents exchanged between OIRA and the agency will be publicly available.

rubrics_metrics.name: How outside parties can notify OIRA of views
rubrics_metrics.description: Best ways: submit comments directly to the agency during the proposed rule stage (Federal Register/Regulations.gov), provide written comments to the OIRA Administrator during review, or request a meeting with the Administrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visit the EO 12866 Meeting Request page to request a meeting; OIRA maintains a log of meetings and posts written materials received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reginfo.gov vs Regulations.gov distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Reginfo.gov provides information about the status of agency documents undergoing OIRA review; Regulations.gov is a portal for the public to review and comment on published regulatory actions and view supporting materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft documents under OIRA review are deliberative and not publicly available; Regulations.gov hosts published proposals and associated comment opportunities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose of a RIN
rubrics_metrics.description: A RIN (Regulation Identifier Number) is assigned by OMB's electronic docketing system to identify each regulatory action listed in the Unified Agenda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies are asked to include RINs in the headings of their Rule and Proposed Rule documents to facilitate tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRA provides the statutory framework for federal collections of information, aiming to (1) minimize paperwork/reporting burdens on the public and (2) ensure maximum possible utility from collected information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PRA requires agencies to seek public comment on proposed information collections and submit proposed collections for OMB review and approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as an information collection under the PRA
rubrics_metrics.description: Information is any statement or estimate of fact or opinion, regardless of form or format, including forms, written reports, surveys, recordkeeping requirements, and third-party/public disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRA applies when identical questions or reporting/recordkeeping requirements are imposed on ten or more 'persons' (individuals, businesses, or state/local/tribal governments); it applies to voluntary and mandatory collections, including those tied to benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Collection Request (ICR) contents
rubrics_metrics.description: An ICR is an agency request for OMB approval of an information collection and includes a description of the collection and planned use, information collection instruments (forms/surveys/scripts), and supporting documentation demonstrating compliance with PRA requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ICRs may include instruments and supporting documentation; where associated with proposed rules certain contents are not public until OMB review is complete and rules are published.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA actions on ICRs
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA can: Approve, mark Improperly Submitted, accept Withdrawal, or Disapprove an ICR. OIRA can approve collections for up to three years and may approve with or without change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ICRs related to proposed rules, OMB may 'file comment' instructing agencies to resubmit at final stage; if disapproved, the agency may not proceed and no person is subject to penalty for noncompliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process to obtain OMB approval of an information collection
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps: agency develops the collection; publishes a Federal Register notice giving 60 days for public comment; considers comments and revises as appropriate; submits the ICR to OMB and publishes a second notice providing 30 more days to comment; OIRA reviews and approves or takes other action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under certain circumstances agencies may request 'emergency' review/approval with explanation and consultation with the public; OMB may modify or waive public comment requirements in these cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: What OMB evaluates during ICR review
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB evaluates whether the collection: is necessary for the proper performance of agency functions and has practical utility; minimizes Federal information-collection burden (especially on those most adversely affected); and maximizes practical utility and public benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA also reviews consistency with laws, regulations, and policies related to privacy, confidentiality, security, information quality, and statistical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: How the public can participate in ICR review
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public should monitor sponsoring agencies' Federal Register notices seeking comments on collections and may submit feedback to agencies and OIRA; the ICR Dashboard lists collections under review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Members may submit comments on currently approved collections at any time; comments can address need for information and reporting burdens.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to submit comments on an information collection (procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal Register notices seeking comment provide submission methods; comments can be submitted to OIRA for consideration during the first 30 days of review via the Comment button on the View ICR - Agency Submission page; a list of ICRs open for comment is on the Information Collection Review page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For comments outside the FR time frame, contact the sponsoring agency directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential Business Information (CBI) and submissions via Reginfo.gov
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit information whose disclosure is restricted by statute (trade secrets, commercial/financial information) to www.reginfo.gov; comments submitted through www.reginfo.gov cannot be claimed as CBI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submitting via Reginfo.gov waives any CBI claims for that submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: How comments are used and disclosure expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: By submitting comments through Reginfo.gov you consent to their use and consideration; electronic comments are maintained in ROCIS and OIRA is the official custodian. Information (including PII) included in comments may be publicly disclosed when OIRA concludes review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact OIRA to verify receipt; contact information provided with comments submitted online will not be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov and may only be used by OIRA. Reginfo.gov provides XML data that may include commenter name if posted by an agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICR Dashboard: types of information-collection requests
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICR Dashboard displays seven types: New collection; Revision; Extension without change; Reinstatement without change; Reinstatement with change; Existing collection in use without OMB Control Number; Discontinue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions explain when each type is used (e.g., revisions for statute-required changes; extensions every three years; discontinuances when collection no longer necessary). Non-material/non-substantive changes are considered technical and do not require public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information available on Reginfo.gov about collections
rubrics_metrics.description: Reginfo.gov shows basic details (title, burden hours). Clicking OMB Control Number shows OMB review history; clicking ICR Reference Number shows the ICR details and instruments (except when contents are linked to a proposed/final regulation — then not public until OMB review completed and rules published).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This allows stakeholders to view review history and supporting materials when available.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA's privacy role in Executive Branch policy
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA provides assistance to Federal agencies on privacy matters, develops Federal privacy policy, and oversees implementation of privacy policy by agencies under statutes such as the Privacy Act, PRA, and E-Government Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicates OIRA's authority and role in privacy, confidentiality, and related policy areas relevant to information collections and rulemaking.
